_comment: ONE definition of what the SERVER accepts, consumed by both sides of the mirror.
TypeScript: tests/emailPolicy.test.ts asserts emailPolicy agrees with serverAccepts on every row.
Python:     scripts/service_text_reference.py RE-DERIVES serverAccepts by calling the pinned
Django's validate_email, and refuses to run at all if Django is absent or is not the
version implementation/api/pyproject.toml pins. It never falls back to a copy of the
client's rule -- the previous version did, and a copy can only ever agree with itself.
serverAccepts is Django 6.1 validate_email() applied to _normalize_email(address) == (raw or '').strip().lower().
The `divergence` tag names a class where Django <=5.1 and Django 6.1 give DIFFERENT answers.
The script asserts every named class has at least one row, AND that the row really does
discriminate -- rows inside the agreeing region cannot detect a wrong transcription, which
is exactly how the first version of this file shipped two wrong verdicts.
Do not edit a verdict by hand. Re-derive it: service_text_reference.py --regenerate

cases.note: an ordinary address
normalised (stripped and lowercased) before validation
plus-tagging, which the client must never reject
a dotted local part and a deep domain
a long modern TLD
an internal hyphen is fine
the shortest real address shape
a digit is fine in a NON-final label, unlike the TLD
the RFC quoted-string local part
Django allowlists bare localhost
IDN domain. The first mirror REJECTED this and Django accepts it -- a customer locked out of every auth surface by a client-only rule
IDN domain, accented first label
IDN TLD: `ul` is part of the TLD class, so a two-character accented TLD is valid
the punycode form of the same domain
digits are legal in a TLD ONLY through the xn-- alternative
an astral code point is OUTSIDE `ul` (which stops at U+FFFF). Python compares code points; JavaScript needs the /u flag to agree, because both halves of the surrogate pair fall inside the range
an all-digit TLD. Django <=5.1 ACCEPTED this and 6.1 rejects it; the first fixture recorded it as accepted, which is the defect this whole class exists for
`.com` typed with a zero -- the TLD class is letters and `ul` only
a digit at the end of the TLD
a LEADING hyphen in the TLD. Django <=5.1 accepted it, 6.1 refuses it, and the first fixture pinned it as accepted WITH A NOTE explaining the wrong behaviour
a trailing hyphen in the TLD
EmailValidator uses tld_no_fqdn_re, so the trailing dot of a fully qualified name is not allowed in an address
exactly 320 characters -- the RFC 3696 limit, accepted
321 characters. Refused by len(value) > 320 before the address is parsed at all; the first mirror had no length check
the IPv4 literal form
literal SHAPE, impossible octets. literal_regex matches and validate_ipv46_address then rejects -- the first mirror checked shape only and accepted it
three octets: shaped like a literal, not an address
a leading zero. CPython dropped the octal reading, so IPv4Address raises
the IPv6 literal form
a compressed IPv6 literal
an IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal
two `::` runs is ambiguous and Python refuses it
39 characters -- exactly MAX_IPV6_ADDRESS_LENGTH, accepted
40 characters. Django caps the TEXT length before parsing, so this is refused for its length

the tagged IPv6 form a reader would expect the dead branch to be about. Django has no such branch -- `I`, `P` and `v` are not in [A-F0-9:.] -- and it is rejected. NOT tagged as a divergence: the invented branch required DOUBLED brackets, so it never matched this either, and a row both rules reject proves nothing about the difference between them

the shape the invented `[IPv6:...]` branch actually matched -- nested brackets. The old reference-script rule ACCEPTED this and Django rejects it, which is what makes this the row that discriminates. The client's copy of the branch was dead twice over: nested brackets AND a case-sensitive `IPv6` tested against an already-lowercased domain
Django rsplits on the LAST at-sign, which is the only reason a quoted local part containing one works. An implementation splitting on the FIRST at-sign rejects this, so the row discriminates
an unquoted second at-sign: the dot-atom class has no `@`, so this is refused however it is split
U+0130 lowercases to `i` PLUS a combining dot above -- two characters, so the TLD clears the {2,63} minimum it would fail as one
the Kelvin sign lowercases to a plain `k`: a one-character TLD, refused
a title-case digraph lowercases to a single character, refused for length
PR #17 (Cody): a one-character TLD, the truncated-TLD typo
PR #17 (Cody): a double-tapped dot
PR #17 (Cody): a leading hyphen in a domain label
PR #17 (Cody): a trailing hyphen in a domain label
no dot in the domain at all
nothing after the at-sign
nothing before the at-sign
no at-sign at all
empty
a space in the local part
a space in the domain
consecutive dots in the local part
a leading dot in the local part
a trailing dot in the local part
a space inside the quoted local part is NOT permitted
a non-ASCII local part: `ul` is in the DOMAIN classes only

U+017F LONG S in the LOCAL part. `ul` is a DOMAIN-side range and this is not it: Django's user_regex carries re.IGNORECASE, and Python's IGNORECASE is FULL CASE FOLDING, so the ASCII letter class silently contains this code point -- and `.lower()` leaves it alone, so it survives normalisation and reaches the class. The client's transcription of that class omitted it and refused the address on all four auth surfaces
U+0131 DOTLESS I, the ordinary Turkish letter, in the local part. Same fold, and the reason this class is a customer lockout rather than a curiosity

the same fold in the QUOTED-STRING alternative. Django's `!#-[` and `]-\177` classes span the ASCII letters too, so all three local-part classes gain it -- swept against the installed 6.1.1 user_regex three times, against `x`, `"x"` and `"\x"`, with the same result

the NEGATIVE control for that fold. U+0130 matches user_regex too, but `_normalize_email` lowercases first and it becomes `i` + U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE, which the class does not contain. Rejected. Without this row, adding the whole folded set instead of the two that survive normalisation would look correct
the other half of that control: U+212A KELVIN SIGN lowercases to a plain `k`, so this is accepted -- as an ordinary `k`, by a class that never had to change. Normalisation does the work, not the fold
a domain label over the 63-character limit
